analysis.title: Global Strategy Weekly: As the bond market bares its teeth, it's not a good time to be swimming naked
key_insights: Albert Edwards says the 2026 global bond bear market may be driven more by a downturn in the global liquidity cycle than by macro fundamentals, and asks whether equities are next.
10y French bond yields have risen above 5% amid concern over what recent riots in France mean for the fiscal arithmetic.

Edwards sees a long secular bear market for bonds, the mirror image of the 1980-2020 Ice Age thesis, and says it could be the backdrop for decades. Larry Jeddeloh's 10% US 10y target is for a couple of cycles out, not this cycle.
Clients are being told 5% yields are the old normal and that negative post-Covid yields were the last gasp of a QE/ZIRP-driven bond bubble.

Government interest payments as a ratio to government revenues is the key fiscal-vulnerability metric per Ed Ballsdon and Ray Dalio. On this measure the US is in a much worse position than other major sovereigns.

The report names the UK, France, US and China as the four worst fiscal positions. The report notes China's current primary deficit is very large, and contrasts today's deficits with the large government surpluses of the late 1990s tech bubble.
US net interest payments are close to 4% of GDP and France's are deteriorating rapidly toward 3%.

Dalio notes US debt burdens are at their highest since WWII and are expected to worsen, with a large amount of maturing debt to roll over. SG Fixed Income says the UK and Japan look relatively safe on the roll-over measure and the US does not.
The UK gilt market is especially exposed to higher inflation, per the OBR Fiscal and Sustainability Report, so it cannot inflate its way out of debt.

The OECD says the investor base of major bond markets has shifted toward more fickle investors, with France most at risk and Japan least. The IMF Investor Risk Index has risen across most major sovereigns since 2023, with France and Italy standing out and Japan's high debt mitigated by a stable investor base.
Under IMF shock scenarios, US debt-to-GDP in 2028 rises in every case, from 131.3 baseline to 135.1 under growth/inflation -1pp.

SG Rates doubts the IMF's France path, which assumes a meaningful primary balance improvement. Using SG economists' primary balance forecasts gives a significantly steeper debt trajectory, especially with weaker growth or fiscal slippage.

David Howell of CrossBorder Capital warns the excess liquidity tide is going out as a robust real economy and heavy demands on capital markets drain liquidity. Edwards presents a chart of China's credit impulse leading the US equity market lower.
